summary: My SHOULD-FIX landed and the repair goes past what I asked: the lead replacement now consumes the evidence clause, and the source-pin cell I raised only secondarily is fixed in the same pass. The repair also surfaced a hazard I had not tested — the shorter DR-G01–G05/G12/G17 token occurs twice, on DR-123 and on DR-129 — and the entry names it, targets the full cell instead, and adds a refusal to touch the DR-129 pin. I verified all of that against live bytes: both replacement targets occur exactly once and each is byte-identical to the entire cell it replaces, which is a stronger property than any target in this series has had. The condition-2 block is byte-identical to turn 1, so its verified fragment preservation carries through. There are no unrequested deletions this turn, which breaks a four-entry habit.

Both replacement targets equal entire cells rather than substrings of them, which I verified by column-parsing the live DR-123 row and comparing each cell to its fenced block. That removes any question of a replacement spilling into or stopping short of a cell boundary, and it is a stronger property than the partial-cell targets used in D-085, D-089 and D-091.

All five fenced blocks extract byte-exactly and behave as expected against live file 08: the two targets at one occurrence each, and the three replacement texts at zero, which is correct for new text.

The header also keeps 'The independent review of this entry is the SATISFIED-GRADE review D-056 Eligibility (4) requires for this row', which four prior repair turns in this family had dropped — the habit I noted at D-085, D-089 and D-091 does not recur here.

consentNote: I CONSENT with zero MUST-FIX and zero SHOULD-FIX. The repair does the thing I asked and then does the thing I only gestured at, and in the course of widening it the coordinator hit a hazard I had not tested: the short G17 token appears on DR-129 as well as DR-123, so the obvious edit would have reached a deferred row this entry has no authority over. I checked that claim rather than accepting it — the token does occur twice — and the entry's answer is right, targeting whole cells and refusing the DR-129 pin explicitly. Both targets turn out to be byte-identical to the entire cells they replace, which is the cleanest targeting in this series of four; the earlier entries all replaced substrings. The condition-2 block did not change, so its preservation of three predecessors' remainders rests on last turn's comparison rather than a fresh one. Worth recording at the close: this is the first repair turn in the family that deletes nothing unrequested, and it keeps the gate-4 declaration that four prior ones dropped.
